aiWorkflow.title: AI-Assisted Workflow
aiWorkflow.intro: I don't just incorporate AI to design and deliver more efficiently — I built a process around it, one I keep refining. Here's how a project actually moves through my hands, from a rough idea to a delivered interface. These processes are in constant evolution.
aiWorkflow.closing: At every step, I'm the one deciding what and how it moves forward. AI does the heavy lifting — not the directing.

workflow.heading: The Real Workflow
workflow.contextLine: *A single loop can take 15 minutes or several hours, depending on the complexity.

helps.heading: Where AI helps
items: Generating variations (three hero-section directions for a client — hours, not days)
Compressing weeks of work into days

doesnt.heading: Where it doesn't
items: Making the call instead of the designer

workflow.closing: Creativity, taste, and judgment — the three things AI still can't do. Those are exactly the three I'm doubling down on.

builtWith.body: This site was designed and built with the workflow above — Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, bilingual, tested, deployed on Vercel. It is the same process, run on my own product instead of a client's.

cta.body: This is how I'd work with your team.

steps.body: In the most 'human' stage, I start by understanding the product and its overall ecosystem: talking with business stakeholders and users, analyzing competitors and the existing market, understanding the needs to be covered. No rigid methodologies: I keep it flexible and follow what each project actually needs.

I convert all that information into guide documents: a written functional brief and a visual direction with references, mood, constraints. This is key to preventing everything that follows from becoming generic.

steps.lead: Design system & concept — Claude Design/Figma Make.
steps.body: With the brief as context, I generate a first basic design system and visual concept. I review it, keep what works, redo what doesn't.

I move to Claude Code (or any AI-assisted Agent/IDE) to start defining the tech stack, architecture, and a staged build plan. Here there must be strong contact with the technical team to ensure the plan is realistic and scalable. The idea is not to rush and throw out garbage code that will later need to be redone, but to plan the project and start with a solid, scalable foundation.
Execution happens in stages (or in parallel), checkpoint by checkpoint. Result: a functional first version, not a mockup.
I quickly validate it — with users or stakeholders when possible — identify critical improvement points, and apply the necessary changes.
Once the product gains some solidity, it may be necessary to sync the UI and design system with Figma, via Chrome extension or MCP, to be able to evolve and scale the design as the product grows.

team.heading: How does this fit into a team?
team.body: Strip away the specific tools and what's left is just good process: a written brief before building anything, a design system as the single source of truth, a review checkpoint between each stage. This works whether it's me and Claude, or a full team on Figma and Jira with no AI involved. The tools change. The discipline doesn't.

caseLink.body: See the same loop run end to end by one person, measurement included:

artifact.alt: VS Code showing this repo's docs folder — ARCHITECTURE, CODING_STANDARDS, CONTENT_MODEL, DESIGN_SYSTEM, IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN, PROJECT_BRIEF — with DESIGN_SYSTEM.md open on its accent-colour usage rules
artifact.caption: What those guiding documents look like in practice, on this very site: what an agent reads before writing a line of code. The accent rules are, in the file's own words, hard constraints, not suggestions.

steps.body: Before any code gets generated, I make sure the Figma file is actually code-ready: tokens (color, spacing, typography) defined as variables, components built with proper Auto Layout, clear states, and naming conventions an AI agent can parse without guessing. A messy file produces messy code — this step isn't optional.

I set up the AI agent (Figma MCP + Claude Code, or a similar setup) with the project's real tech stack, folder structure, and coding conventions — the component library in use, naming patterns, existing architecture. Without this, the agent fills the gaps with assumptions, and assumptions mean rework.

Design tokens get exported from Figma before a single component is touched — colors, spacing, typography become the single source of truth shared between Figma and the codebase, so nothing gets hardcoded downstream.

With tokens in place, I generate the smallest building blocks first — buttons, inputs, cards — matched 1:1 to their Figma counterparts, including every interactive state (hover, disabled, error, loading). No component moves forward until it holds up against spec.

From there, components climb the Atomic Design ladder: base components combine into molecules, then organisms, then full screens — always validated against the Figma layout, never generated in one uncontrolled pass.

All AI-generated code lands in its own branch, never directly on main. Developers review and merge it through GitHub pull requests, exactly like any other contribution — AI speeds up the first draft, the team still owns quality control.

Once merged, I keep the Figma file and the live component library aligned, so design and code don't drift apart as the product grows. Same discipline as keeping tokens in sync on the way in, applied on the way back out.

team.heading: Handoff Process
team.body: AI-generated code goes through the same review process as any other pull request. This requires synchronization with the development team and speaking their language.

prompting.intro: Prompt engineering as a craft is fading. The models got good enough that elaborate prompting buys almost nothing — and the guidance now coming out of the labs themselves says the same: describe the task, set the limits, define what “done” looks like, then get out of the way. What’s left was never really about the model. It’s knowing what you’re asking for, and how you’ll know it’s right.

structure.heading: What a strong prompt still needs

items.label: The task
items.body: What to build. It can be ambitious — the model holds it now.

items.label: Guardrails
items.body: What it must not touch, invent, or hardcode.

items.label: Done when
items.body: The finish line, and how it verifies itself against it.

items.label: Let it run
items.body: No step-by-step babysitting. Review the result, not the route.

context.label: Before the prompt
context.body: None of this starts from zero. The agent is already loaded with the project’s context — stack and folder structure, the team’s coding standards, the design system rules — set up once and shared by everyone working on the repo. The prompt only carries what’s specific to this task.

example.lead: A real request from the Hard Rock migration, rewritten the way I’d write it today. My old version of this was three times longer: an assigned role, tone instructions, worked examples, the conventions restated inline. None of that earns its place anymore. This does:
example.code:
Migrate the Planner filter bar from Figma to code.

TASK
Pull the component from Figma over MCP: [link to component].
Build it in src/components/planner/, matching every state
defined in the file.

GUARDRAILS
Follow the coding standards and design system rules already
in context — don't restate or reinterpret them.
Tokens only: no hardcoded hex, px or font sizes.
Reuse Button and Select from the existing library.
Touch nothing outside src/components/planner/.

DONE WHEN
Every Figma state renders: default, focus, disabled, loading, error.
pnpm test and pnpm build pass.
Visual diff against the Figma frame is under 2%.

Check all three yourself before handing it back.

prompting.closing: Writing that prompt took four minutes. Knowing what belonged under DONE WHEN took fifteen years. That’s the part that doesn’t get automated.
